meta.title: Who Is Shaping Your Home? Inside Xiaohongshu’s Interior Design Culture
meta.desc: From the factories of Foshan to apartments in Taipei: how Xiaohongshu and Taobao are rewriting what a Taiwanese home is supposed to look like — and what that costs the people who make furniture for a living.

strings.cap1: △ Interiors in every imaginable style, as served up by Xiaohongshu.
strings.cap2: △ At the 2026 China (Guangzhou) International Building and Decoration Fair, exhibitors pitched their newest AI products to buyers: whole-home AI systems, AI design platforms, even AI mood lighting.
strings.cap4: △ Customer-service staff handling enquiries before and after a sale. If a buyer complains to the platform, Taobao can shut a shop down, freeze its payments or throttle its traffic.
strings.cap5: △ Overtime is the norm in Foshan’s furniture factories, where workers get two to four days off a month. Behind every station — carpentry, cutting, sewing, upholstery, assembly, inspection, packing, shipping — is a household depending on it.
strings.cap6: △ A furniture building in Foshan’s Longjiang township, with five or six factories stacked inside. Yang Yao says the barrier to entry is low: cover a few months’ rent, hire some workers, lay in materials, and tens of thousands of yuan is enough to open a factory.
strings.cap7: △ Mismatched timber and cushions dumped straight onto the floor: the raw materials and the housekeeping at a budget Taobao sofa factory both betray a quality gap that custom workshops do not have.
strings.cap8: △ The sofa in Jang Won-young’s home. (Source: Jang Won-young’s Instagram.)
strings.cap9: △ Showrooms in Foshan exist so factories can demonstrate what they can build and how far they can customise it. They are also where buyers are received — wholesalers, retailers and interior designers, domestic and foreign — and where orders are negotiated.
strings.cap10: △ Foshan is also home to media agencies built around the furniture and home-furnishing trade, selling industry coverage, brand exposure and marketing campaigns.
strings.cap11: △ At the 2026 Guangzhou fair, stand after stand had been turned into a livestreaming set, selling on camera from the show floor.
strings.cap12: △ A workers’ dormitory at a furniture factory in Guangdong. Yang Yao’s plant sits outside the furniture clusters, so he provides housing to hold on to skilled migrant workers — the opposite of Longjiang and Lecong, where craftsmen rent their own rooms and change employers at will.
strings.cap13: △ Many Taiwanese factories now buy half-finished pieces from Taobao, supervise the work remotely by video call, then ship them home for finishing and refinishing — a different way of selling furniture.
strings.cap14: △ Furniture factories in Wugu, New Taipei, once supplied local retailers wholesale. As the internet and shopping habits changed, some have moved to fully bespoke work. The sofas on the showroom floor are not stock but demonstrations of craft and technique; occasionally a walk-in customer can buy one outright.
strings.p1: Xiaohongshu is a Chinese social platform built around images, and there is almost nothing it does not cover. On home design alone, its creators have posted millions of times, turning domestic space into something to be photographed, displayed and shared. The shift accelerated after the pandemic. As remote work spread and people spent more hours at home, the definition of a good living space stretched beyond durability and function to take in visual appeal — and how well a room photographs.
strings.p2: Taobao, the Chinese e-commerce platform, supplies the logistics behind that appetite: cheap goods in enormous variety. Whether shoppers reverse-image-search a photograph to find the same piece or simply tap a link embedded in a Xiaohongshu post, the ideal interior has never been easier to copy.
strings.p3: “When you’ve hired a Taiwanese designer and a crew, and you realise you’re paying good money to suffer, you start thinking: why not just go and dig it up on Taobao yourself?” Shaobai asks.
strings.p4: He had grown tired of all of it — briefing designers, coordinating carpenters and electricians, comparing one contractor’s quote against another’s. So when his new place was ready, he skipped the whole exhausting business. He opened ChatGPT and typed in a few words describing the style he wanted.
strings.p5: In under ten seconds, a set of <button class="term" type="button" data-term="3D渲染圖">3D renderings</button> appeared, laid over his actual floor plan and looking exactly like the “Bauhaus” rooms on Xiaohongshu. Shaobai studied the geometry and the clean lines, and began picturing the paintings, the cabinets, the rugs — what the place would become once everything was in position. Within minutes he had settled on what to buy. “Mostly I’m checking Taobao to see whether the price blows my budget. If it’s too expensive, I go looking for a <button class="term" type="button" data-term="平替">dupe</button>.”
strings.p6: “At this point I basically can’t buy furniture in a physical shop any more.” Shaobai is 43. He used to work in semiconductors and ran a Shopee storefront on the side, making his margin on the spread; today he is a tattoo artist. Those years of online reselling shaped how he shops, leaving him far more comfortable buying sight-unseen than most people his age. To Xiaobei, a homemaker approaching 60, it is almost unimaginable.
strings.p7: The most furniture Xiaobei ever bought at once was more than thirty years ago, when she married and moved into a new apartment. At a shop on the outskirts of Hsinchu she bought a full set of solid-wood pieces — chest of drawers, bed frame, dining table, dressing table — for around NT$200,000, part of the dowry from her family. The couple hired no designer. They asked relatives and friends what they thought, then went to the shop and chose.
strings.p8: Three decades on, housing prices have swallowed most people’s savings, and a severe labour shortage means renovation crews are booked three or four months out, sometimes half a year. Skipping the designer is still a common choice. What has changed is where people look instead: more and more of them now treat Xiaohongshu as the source of their ideas.
strings.p9: Open the app and a slogan greets you: “Your community of life and interests.” That is what it is — a vast, constantly replenished archive of the everyday. Under the home-design tab, the posts arrive wrapped in style labels: cream, French light-luxury, wabi-sabi, Muji, dopamine, “ins.” No training is required. Follow the trending tags and the templates, and a stock of visual references is yours, ready to be copied and pasted into a home.
strings.p10: Style is only the beginning. Xiaohongshu has also generated a vocabulary for particular households and temperaments: #pet-proofing, #age-proofing, #child-proofing, #lazy-proofing. The tags answer to pets as family members, to the mobility and daily needs of older residents, to children’s safety and growth, or simply to the wish for a life with less effort in it. Each one compresses a tangle of design decisions into a template a shopper can apply without thinking.
strings.p11: Alongside them runs an enormous body of posts tagged #allkillnofiller, #nosecrets, #stepbystep. Some show you how to transform a wall without touching the structure; others walk you through bulbs of different colour temperatures and fixtures of different kinds, so you can “say goodbye to dead white light.” Advice grounded in experience means users are no longer dependent on a designer. They have more say over their own homes.
strings.p12: As AI and whole-home systems spread, another expectation has attached itself to the domestic interior: it should not merely look good, it should “know you better than you know yourself.” Smart switches, smart lighting, smart climate control, smart appliances — a butler in software form, working its way into ordinary life and, in Xiaohongshu’s telling, repackaged as the baseline equipment of a modern household.
strings.p13: The platform’s pull extends beyond young renters doing up a flat and first-time buyers. Interior designer Lin Ting-yu says clients in their forties and fifties now forward her Xiaohongshu posts during design consultations. Last December the Ministry of the Interior imposed a one-year order suspending domain resolution and restricting access to the platform. The desktop version stopped working; the app was untouched, and for users in Taiwan the practical effect has been slight.
strings.p14: “I scroll when I hide in the toilet at work. That little thrill of stolen time suits short posts perfectly.” Anson’s day job is as a network engineer; on the side he runs an independent clothing label. The day job, as he sees it, is not where his talents or his enthusiasms live, and he is unembarrassed about the occasional stretch of slacking off, or of moonlighting on company time.
strings.p15: When he first saw a classmate watching videos about searing steak during a graduate seminar, Anson could not see the appeal, and did not think he needed information from China. Then he stumbled onto the platform’s styling and fashion content, and found himself drawn in. “I like the feeling of information being dense. Some questions get you nothing useful on Google, but on Xiaohongshu there’s an answer.”
strings.p16: Two years after graduating, Anson started following posts about desk setups, and the algorithm widened its recommendations into interiors and renovation. What captivated him most, though, was not online at all: it was his grandmother’s room, in what Xiaohongshu users call “Republican-era style.” The reference points are Chiang Kai-shek’s residence and Sun Yat-sen’s former home — an aesthetic of East-meets-West, dark timber in quantity, and ornament everywhere; a look with more lived-in texture and sense of period than the minimalism contemporary design chases. That style gradually became his picture of an ideal home, and his first rented flat in Taipei became what he calls the MVP — the minimum viable product — of that picture.
strings.p17: One bedroom, one living room, one bathroom. Standing in the entryway, you catch the voice of Laufey, the Icelandic-Chinese singer-songwriter, leaking through the bedroom door — retro, warm, somehow still modern — and find yourself slowing down. Anson pushes the door open more gently than he needs to. A projector throws its beam across the room in soft amber, and something in you lets go before you have decided to.
strings.p18: Looking at the care that has gone into the place, it is hard to picture what he started with: close to a bare shell, no furniture, no partitions, the bathroom plumbed but without a basin or a toilet. For a tenant hoping to move in with a single suitcase, it would have been a nightmare. For Anson it was a windfall. Back in his dorm years he had followed the crowd to Muji for storage boxes, only to be disappointed — the room was tidier, but tidiness was nowhere near beauty. For someone this exacting about how things look, the Xiaohongshu notion of a “mess tolerance rate” was what prompted him to rethink what made a space beautiful.
strings.p19: What he wanted, Anson says, was not a room that looked good when it was tidy, but one that held its looks while it was being lived in, with things left lying about. “My books, my clutter — they don’t have to go back on a shelf. Put them down anywhere and it still looks right. That’s mess tolerance.” Traditional Taiwanese renovation, he adds, loves a wall of built-in cabinetry: plenty of storage, but the moment the things left out are not put away, the room falls apart.
strings.p20: The furniture in Anson’s flat comes from everywhere: an IKEA sofa picked up on Facebook Marketplace and Shopee, old pieces from the family house in Taichung — a record player, an electric fan — and a few things dug out of Taobao.
strings.p21: Taobao sellers stuff their listings with keywords so shoppers can find them. One reads “Japanese Muji white oak coat rack freestanding solid wood quality hanger guesthouse bedroom special offer”: a copy of Muji’s acacia entryway rack, which sells officially in Taiwan for NT$3,990. The Taobao version uses cheaper pine, hence the gap. Another — “black stainless steel magazine rack bookshelf Bauhaus sofa side cabinet living room storage Japanese floor stand bedside cabinet” — copies Muji’s SUS shelving. Anson points at it. “The original doesn’t come in this many colours, and the standard range doesn’t include accessories like the magazine rack. On Taobao you can order those separately.” For him the platform is not only the cheaper option; it fills in what the original brand will not offer in finish, colour and fittings.
strings.p22: Taobao arrived in Taiwan as early as 2009, but it did not visibly shift spending until around 2014 and 2015. As Singles’ Day, cross-border logistics and payment services became familiar, the platform moved from a niche for dedicated online shoppers to a mainstream route for buying from abroad. In late 2024 Taobao put NT$2 billion into shipping subsidies for Singles’ Day alone; Taipei Metro platforms, walls and carriages were papered with the campaign, free delivery and discounts repeating down the length of the train — a measure of how deliberately the company was positioning itself in Taiwan.
strings.p23: For many Chinese manufacturers, Taiwan has stopped being simply one more market. It is a proving ground before going further abroad: whether a product holds up here is taken, to a degree, as a verdict on the brand and on what it makes.
strings.p24: Xiao Ma, a certified corporate trainer for Alibaba, puts it this way: “Taiwanese consumers are relatively demanding about quality, and the testing and regulatory standards are strict. So for mainland sellers, a product that clears the Taiwanese market comes with an extra layer of endorsement.” That track record is then recycled as marketing material when the same firms push into Southeast Asia and beyond, to blunt doubts about quality in markets that do not know them.
strings.p25: “Something that sells for just over NT$200 on Taobao can go for NT$500 or NT$600 by the time it reaches Taiwan.” To Hsu Hsin, then a first-year political science undergraduate in 2020, that was an opening worth taking. Her field of study left her uneasy about Beijing’s softer forms of influence, but it did not stop her and a friend from buying clothes wholesale and reselling them on Shopee for the margin.
strings.p26: “I’m a bit compulsive about comparing prices.” If the goods come out of the same factory, she reasons, there must be a cheaper listing somewhere. “Sometimes the difference is NT$10 or NT$20 and I still can’t stop until I’ve found the best price.” Six years in, Hsu Hsin has worked out a method of her own, and it does not begin on Taobao. It begins on Shopee, which she treats as a filter: Taiwanese sellers have already screened for style and quality, so she finds something she likes there, screenshots it, and takes the image back to Taobao to hunt down the source factory or a cheaper seller.
strings.p27: With all those checks in place, the only real drawback left is the shipping time. If she needs something immediately she orders on Shopee and pays for next-day delivery. If she can wait, she almost always goes back to Taobao, where the same item is usually noticeably cheaper.
strings.p28: What she buys ranges widely — clothes, computer peripherals, household goods, even the parts her father needed to repair a car. That range has always been one of Taobao’s strengths, and it is also what trips up newcomers: when every product returns hundreds of thousands of results, you need a system for avoiding the duds. Hsu Hsin reads buyer reviews closely and studies the photographs other customers upload, checking for differences in colour, size and cut. “The price is low, so I was never expecting much on quality,” she says. “Even when it turns out worse than I hoped, it doesn’t really sting.”
strings.p29: She has also watched the platform change in how it treats Taiwan. The buying process, first of all, has become far easier. “In the early days you had to find your own <button class="term" type="button" data-term="私人集運">private consolidator</button>, and tracking order numbers and shipments was a nuisance. Now Taobao runs a service where RMB 99 gets you <button class="term" type="button" data-term="包郵">free shipping</button> to Taiwan, items from different shops are combined automatically, and it comes to your door.”
strings.p30: Service has changed too. Sellers once ignored enquiries written in traditional Chinese characters. Now many reply quickly, deal with after-sales problems willingly, and volunteer coupons and discounts. Electronics listings increasingly specify Taiwanese standards and voltage, and product names have begun to carry the search terms Taiwanese shoppers actually use. “Their messages sometimes start with ‘hon’ or ‘sis’, so it feels friendlier,” Hsu Hsin says, mimicking the customer-service patter down to the inflection.
strings.p31: Taobao furniture, though, did not take hold at the same pace as the platform itself. By the mid-2010s, Taiwanese forums were carrying accounts of buying large pieces from Taobao, but cross-border freight, shipping costs and after-sales problems kept it to a handful of adventurous shoppers. After 2020 the pandemic pushed spending indoors and online; Taobao improved its logistics and after-sales service and, in 2021, launched an end-to-end furniture service that bundled inspection, consolidated freight, delivery and in-home assembly — all of which buyers had previously had to arrange themselves. Only then did Taobao furniture move from fringe option to something a Taiwanese household might genuinely consider. The price gap against every other channel is wide enough that shoppers will swallow the sea freight.
strings.p32: A-liang, who buys Taobao furniture to order on other people’s behalf, saw the same opening in a platform that kept getting easier to use. He takes his cut on the spread; he also draws on years of accumulated buying to vet quality for his customers. Furniture carries a higher unit price than everyday goods, which makes the gap between Taiwanese and Chinese platforms more visible — so even after freight, his service fee and installation, buying from Taobao still comes out well ahead on price.
strings.p33: Elynne, a soft-furnishings designer with years of experience managing cleaning for luxury apartments, is another devoted Taobao user. She has more than a decade in the cleaning trade and took her first commission as a designer this February. “I photograph the light fittings in my clients’ homes, then go back to Taobao and search for the same piece.” After trying it a few times, she found she could nearly always locate something close, and far cheaper. “Taiwanese furniture shops carry a narrower range and charge a good deal more, and it doesn’t always suit what the client wants.”
strings.p34: Getting burned on Taobao furniture is not reserved for amateurs. Elynne paid her own tuition before she learned the tricks. “These days I only buy pieces rated 4.8 or above, and I check how they’ll be packed before I order.” She remembers an early job: “I took a chance on a 4.7-rated painting for a client and nearly lost a fortune. It was a little cheaper than the others, but when it reached the consolidator we found the seller had used nothing but a soft carton with no protection. The outer packaging was completely destroyed.”
strings.p35: A bad experience has not turned her against the platform. “I don’t think everything on Taobao is junk. You get what you pay for — you just have to know how to choose. The same chair comes at every price point. You need to understand the materials, whether the price is reasonable, whether the seller is sound.”
strings.p36: Experienced shoppers and people in the trade have ways of knowing the going rate and reading the signals. First-time buyers have far less to go on. In recent years, Foshan’s <button class="term" type="button" data-term="頭部家具買家">top-tier furniture buyers</button> — figures such as “Brother Hei” and Sun Yao, active on Facebook, Instagram and Douyin — have built followings, and have begun urging people to skip Taobao altogether and buy in person in Foshan, in Guangdong province, the home base of the factories that list there. Last March, Hu Han-yan, the Hsinchu crane magnate known as the “Crane King,” travelled to Foshan’s Louvre furniture exhibition centre to pick out grand pieces for his newly completed office building, and the trip was widely discussed online. Travel agencies have joined in, packaging tours under headlines like “A hundred million visitors! This Guangdong furniture city is now a national 4A scenic spot.” Between them they have built up an idea — go to the source and you will get furniture at rock-bottom prices — while delivering shoppers who do not know the rules of the trade straight to the people who do.
strings.p37: The Lecong and Longjiang districts of Foshan, in Guangdong, have long gone by the name “ten miles of furniture city” — Lecong for the showrooms and brand storefronts, Longjiang for the factories that make the goods. Yang Yao, who runs a furniture brand, has a 20,000-square-metre plant on the boundary between Guangzhou and Foshan. One industry, he says, feeds the whole district: “Stop anyone on the street. They’re either making furniture or they’re in renovation, coatings, building materials — something attached to it.”
strings.p38: But China’s economy has soured, the property slump has dragged the furniture trade down with it, and in the scramble for orders the whole market has become brutally <button class="term" type="button" data-term="卷">involuted</button>. Browse Taobao and a small single-seat sofa can be had for under NT$200 — low enough that you wonder whether it is a scam. Yet since Yang Yao started posting on Threads this year, buyers keep sending him screenshots of Taobao furniture, asking whether he can get it cheaper at the factory gate.
strings.p39: Yang Yao is a Taiwanese businessman who has run a furniture brand in Foshan for sixteen years. He spent about four years selling furniture in Taiwan before moving to the Foshan market, and now works across mainland China, Southeast Asia and Taiwan. On the Taiwanese side his clients are designers, furniture retailers, factories, restaurant chains and property developments — he rarely deals with individual shoppers at the far end of the chain. He is blunt about the economics: “Taobao furniture is already about as cheap as it gets. You will struggle to find anything below it.”
strings.p40: Consumer psychology has become badly distorted, he argues: everyone is hunting the lowest number, and manufacturers will do whatever it takes to get there. “A lot of Taobao factories use the worst materials they can, then mass-produce to drive the price down.” You get what you pay for, and the risk is the buyer’s to carry. “A lot of the photographs are retouched, and some are lifted straight from the original brand. What arrives looks like the picture but feels nothing like it — and by the time it reaches Taiwan it may be missing screws or fittings.”
strings.p41: One of the sofa factories that lists on Taobao turns out to occupy the third floor of an industrial block. Unlike the plants that work with established distributors, its signboard carries no company name. Taobao furniture factories usually do not have one, Yang Yao explains, and they do not take much space; when business goes badly the owner sometimes simply takes the money and disappears. “Plenty of them have the lowest possible credit rating. Some are <button class="term" type="button" data-term="限高">barred from high-end consumption</button> outright.”
strings.p42: Mr Huang, who owns the factory, greets us warmly and sits us down at the tea table where he does business. He is wearing a white adidas casual top, with none of the distance of a company boss about him — more like an uncle you would visit at New Year. He keeps up a stream of welcome while his hands work without pause: warming the pot, measuring the leaves, pouring, decanting, every step fluent from long repetition.
strings.p43: Mr Huang has more than twenty years in the trade. He started as a contract manufacturer rather than selling on Taobao directly, and the pandemic broke that model for good. Four or five years ago, as the pandemic receded, orders began falling away. Worse, contract work was not only thin on margin; for a factory carrying heavy fixed costs, the strain on cash flow was severe. “A <button class="term" type="button" data-term="貨款">payment</button> might be a million-plus yuan, and from shipping the goods to actually seeing the money is often two months.”
strings.p44: Rather than keep waiting — for orders, then for payment — Mr Huang decided to take the selling back into his own hands. “In the end I stopped doing contract work, split the operation off, built a sales team and sold on Taobao myself.” The factory stopped making things for other people and went looking for customers of its own, which reshaped its finances. At the height of the contract years, whatever the size of any single order, hundreds of thousands of yuan moved through the plant in a day. The margins and the scale now are not comparable. “Everything goes through Taobao. We do about two million yuan a month, maybe 60,000 or 70,000 a day.”
strings.p45: Selling on a platform carries its own exposure: traffic. Staying visible means paying for marketing, and nobody can promise what any given spend will return in orders. “We don’t dare go big, because we’re afraid the promotion money goes in and never comes back. Right now the thinking is just to keep this factory steady.” Rather than chase growth, Mr Huang wants the place to keep running.
strings.p46: Yang Yao does not encourage ordinary consumers to come to Foshan and buy for themselves. Without a reliable contact inside the trade, he says, it is easy to fall into a hole. “The barrier to opening a furniture factory is low and the undercutting is vicious. A lot of owners grab orders for the cash flow, and when the money arrives they don’t start production — they buy a flat or a car. So customers place orders and never get the goods, or get something terrible.”
strings.p47: For a consumer who does not need furniture in quantity, Yang Yao offers a rule of thumb: if you want cheap, go straight to Taobao and accept the risk. If you want serious custom work, the Foshan factories are where the price gap opens up. “A set of Italian furniture might run to a million-odd New Taiwan dollars. Through a proper bespoke workshop in Foshan, you can have it for a bit over a hundred thousand.”
strings.p48: Reproductions are the other thing Foshan is known for.
strings.p49: Yang Yao’s personal assistant, Chen Nuo-yan, is 26, and her social feeds are full of celebrity news. Her eyes light up when the conversation turns to Korean trends. She mentions a sofa in the home of the K-pop star Jang Won-young, worth as much as NT$6 million: the photographs had been circulating online for less than a week before copies appeared in Foshan.
strings.p50: Conditions have sharpened competition across the trade, and the sheer scale of Foshan makes things possible that ought not to be.
strings.p51: The furniture city holds hundreds of thousands of shops and factories. Unremarkable buildings turn out to be full of furniture-making, and the occupants do not only compete — they watch one another. Firms with a little capital club together to fund a showroom for their own pieces, and visiting one means booking ahead so the operators can establish who you are and why you have come. Photography is tightly restricted. On the floor, the sales staff who greet visitors and walk them through the range also keep an eye out for professional cameras and for anyone shooting a single product up close. All of it is meant to reduce the risk of their designs being copied.
strings.p52: “This whole industry just copies off itself.” Ian, who has been in furniture for under a year, says it without much concern.
strings.p53: Ian has worked as a fishing guide abroad and as airline ground staff, and arrived by a roundabout route at a job as product manager for an overseas hotel-furniture company. Its clients were global chains of the Marriott kind. His job was to understand what a hotel needed, take the <button class="term" type="button" data-term="圖紙">drawings</button> supplied by the hotel’s designers, then work the Chinese factories, negotiate a good price and see the pieces made.
strings.p54: Open a client’s drawings and the spreadsheet is strikingly plain: product name, a photograph showing the form, dimensions, material notes. From the image alone, Ian says, a factory can reverse-engineer the piece. The curves, the sheen of the leather and the way it feels to sit on will differ from the original, but visually the match is close — and this is simply how the industry works. “Run the image through a reverse search and you’ll see none of it is original design,” he says, lightly. A large chain orders thousands of tables and chairs at a time. “They care about cost more than they care about intellectual property.”
strings.p55: Yang Yao has taken Taiwanese orders in recent years, and he does not see reproduction as inherently disrespectful to the original. Sometimes it is a matter of fitting local conditions. “The original sofa might use down in the cushions, but Taiwan is so humid that down collapses, so we swap in silk wadding.” Mattress sizes differ between China and Taiwan too, which means adjusting the bed frames to match.
strings.p56: Then there is folk belief. Taiwanese customers care a great deal about the <button class="term" type="button" data-term="文公尺">feng shui ruler</button>, Yang Yao says, and office furniture in particular — desks above all — has to be measured with the tabletop length in mind. Craftsmen avoid the dimensions considered unlucky and land on the ones marked auspicious. “Customers on the mainland side don’t really care.”
strings.p57: Reproductions have themselves split into price tiers, according to fabric, how they sit and what after-sales service comes with them. As the distance between original and copy widens, the copies have developed a competitive logic of their own: sellers no longer differentiate on the product. They pour everything into reaching the right buyer precisely — into being seen, clicked and bought in a market saturated with information.
strings.p58: “Planting grass” is common currency in Chinese social and e-commerce circles: using content, recommendations or shared experience to seed a desire for something. Put plainly, it is about finding the right host for the product. Xiaohongshu is a standard channel for planting Taobao goods; sellers post there with a Taobao link attached, so that out of an ocean of options, theirs is the one a shopper notices.
strings.p59: Yet the platform's ecosystem is built on the “note,” and it rewards something other than instant traffic or a brief viral spike: it rewards whether the content itself — a review, a slice of life, a piece of product information — is genuinely useful and well made. A creator hoping to make a living from sponsored posts therefore needs a clear editorial identity and a steady output of material with real reference value and credibility, built up over time.
strings.p60: Being seen among so many creators was never going to be easy. Most pick a “vertical lane” they are good at and stay in it, narrowing to a particular industry, product category or type of shopper in order to hold an audience. “The creators who thrive on Xiaohongshu are usually the ones who study their rivals’ weak points, then rework them, copy the successful template or engineer the next hit,” says Xiao Ma, the certified Alibaba trainer.
strings.p61: Creators should also be able to analyse specific competitors and the benchmark accounts in their market, he adds — topic selection, cover images, headlines, the structure of the copy — in order to work out what the market responds to. The hashtags threaded through that copy are one way of putting a proven formula to work.
strings.p62: Because of how the platform behaves, advertising alone rarely buys meaningful exposure. So sellers and e-commerce platforms commission short videos from creators, tucking the sales message inside the creator’s own post. It suits what the platform likes to surface, and it substitutes recommendation for pitch, lowering the viewer’s guard and seeding the desire more effectively.
strings.p63: Hsu Hsin does not only work the price gaps on Taobao. She is also a creator with nearly 30,000 followers on Instagram. Last year, she says, a Chinese marketing agency approached her to make short videos for Pinduoduo, another Chinese e-commerce platform. For the videos themselves she chose approachable household objects and unboxed them.
strings.p64: Once the desire has been seeded, the contest moves to online service — and competition is fierce enough that relentless warmth and a faultless manner are no longer a bonus but the baseline. Xiao Ma has watched it up close: “For Alibaba, the window around a major sales event is an intense scramble for customers. Staff will sleep at the office so they can answer price enquiries at any hour.” Set against the Taiwanese instinct for a sustainable life and workload, countless people in China will work 9am to 9pm, six days a week — “996” — or even 7am to 7pm, seven days a week. Weekends included, many of them are in the company dormitory.
strings.p65: The same disposition shows up in how accounts are run. On any platform, suspensions, permanent bans and takedowns are hardly unusual. Some creators appeal through official channels, or rally their followers in the hope that public pressure will force a review. Xiaohongshu creators tend not to bother. Rather than burn time wrestling with the rules, “they accept it, they comply, and they don’t waste a minute complaining about a <button class="term" type="button" data-term="封號">ban</button>. They just go around it and <button class="term" type="button" data-term="起號">start a new account</button>,” Xiao Ma says.
strings.p66: That choice reflects a survival logic worked out in an intensely competitive market: registering again and rebuilding the content and the following is treated as the cheaper, faster option. Xiao Ma puts it without ceremony. “If Taiwanese creators run a Xiaohongshu account the way they’re used to working, they are not going to beat the mainlanders.”
strings.p67: Alice trained as an interior designer and spent years at a conventional Taiwanese design firm. In 2020 she launched her own soft-furnishings label and moved into styling, taking on the partial renovations that full-service firms rarely want. Her brand’s Instagram account has since gathered around 63,000 followers, and she uses it to pass on the home content she finds on Xiaohongshu.
strings.p68: For Alice the platform is a deep well of domestic ideas, and what draws her most is the warmth of lived experience in them. Against the spotless, chilly show-flat photography of traditional Taiwanese design magazines, the homes on Xiaohongshu carry the evidence of use: a sofa that has been sat on, everyday objects left on the dining table. The spaces are not always perfect, and that is precisely what lets her see what people actually need from a home.
strings.p69: “Some of the home products on Xiaohongshu are sold on Taobao too, so it gives me more routes to new suppliers.” Sixteen years into using Taobao, Alice long ago stopped treating it as merely a place to shop; it is where she sources home products, finds new brands and scouts suppliers. Between the two platforms, she says, runs a continuous chain from content to inspiration to goods.
strings.p70: Wugu district, in New Taipei, has always been one of northern Taiwan’s furniture heartlands. At its height it held two or three thousand storefronts. Now there are one or two hundred, and this year alone fifty have closed.
strings.p71: The upheaval in Taiwan’s traditional furniture industry showed itself more than a decade ago, and Yang Yao’s own career traces the migration. Before leaving for China, he went back to Dacun, in Changhua, to work at the traditional furniture plant his uncle had run for more than thirty years. He was put on the front line in sales, criss-crossing the island for the big furniture fairs in the north, the centre and the south, and built up about four years of experience. In 2009, in his early thirties, he took his uncle’s advice and went to China to manage a joint-venture furniture factory. He has been there ever since.
strings.p72: In the glory years of Taiwanese furniture, the trade was more than part of daily life; it was how Taiwan presented itself to the world, and “Made in Taiwan” was a mark the industry wore with some pride.
strings.p73: In the 1970s Taiwan became the world’s largest furniture exporter, and the title “kingdom of furniture” was born. The island had abundant timber, and generations of craftsmen had built up deep woodworking skill, one cut and one chisel-stroke at a time. As global demand grew, Taiwan rode the wave of international production-sharing, and its factories, running modern assembly lines, assembled a complete export-manufacturing system.
strings.p74: In the 1990s the low-cost advantages of Southeast Asia and mainland China came into view, Taiwan’s environmental regulations tightened, and the global map of the industry was redrawn. Craftsmen left the trade, factories moved offshore, and the kingdom’s reputation faded. The traditional furniture businesses still standing today have all come through a difficult reinvention.
strings.p75: Chen Ching-hsiang has spent more than twenty years in furniture sales. He once ran an online storefront and was among the first ten sellers on Yahoo! Auctions, which put him into online furniture retail very early. The Chinese effect on Taiwan’s industry, he reckons, began about a decade ago. Shipping furniture from China once took two to three months by sea; now it is about one. Buyers can even send a design online and have a Chinese factory build to the drawing.
strings.p76: China is not the only pressure. In recent years traditional retailers have also been losing younger customers simply for lack of visibility online. Huang Chen-chang, the general manager of a local furniture business, is the second generation in a family firm; he has run what his father built for more than twenty years.
strings.p77: Dressed in black with a gold chain at his neck, Huang brews Dayuling high-mountain tea at the tea table while he talks about how the market has shifted. China, he argues, is the distant cause; online retailers are the fire at his feet. Because price, quality and after-sales service differ, Chinese and Taiwanese furniture occupy separate segments — so the heaviest blow has come instead from domestic brands that have thrown themselves into selling online. “Take young brands like AJ2, Mr Sofa, Mian Doufu. They spend more than NT$500,000 a month on advertising to build the brand, but with few physical shops their staffing and rent are relatively low, and they can reach customers anywhere in Taiwan,” he says.
strings.p78: The way out, Huang believes, is to go fully digital: photograph everything, list all of it online, keep prices transparent, and let customers buy with confidence.
strings.p79: Visit five furniture shops in Wugu and price the same thing — a two-seat sofa — and the figures run from NT$6,000 to NT$16,000. Customers cannot easily tell what accounts for the difference, and the sales staff appear free to name whatever number they like. This is the familiar bind of shopping in person: the fear of overpaying, set against the fear of buying something shoddy. Not knowing the going rate, many would rather buy from an online shop where other customers’ reviews are visible, with other people’s experience to go on.
strings.p80: Going digital, however, costs money. GAGU, a Wugu furniture brand of thirty-five years’ standing, shut without warning last July amid reports of unpaid wages; the transition had pushed fixed operating costs up sharply while overall demand stayed weak, and the cash flow gave way. Elsewhere, many proprietors are elderly, with less stamina and less fight than they once had, or they own the land their shop sits on and face no immediate financial threat, which makes reinvention feel less than urgent. Like a frog in slowly heating water, the trade as a whole keeps contracting.
strings.p81: Fewer and fewer Taiwanese furniture shops have a second generation, as Huang Chen-chang does, willing to take over. Walk into the traditional wooden-furniture shops of Wugu on a weekday and business is dead; it is when the sales staff take their days off, and some shops have not even switched the lights on, so that the place looks shut. Only when I push the door open does the owner — in his sixties or seventies, hair half grey, reading glasses on — look up to confirm someone has come in, and get to his feet to turn on a few lights, so the customer is not left feeling shut out.
strings.p82: Whether he could tell I was not about to buy anything, or whether he had simply lost the enthusiasm he once had for his own stock, he skipped even the small talk and let me wander the shop with barely a word.
strings.p83: In China the same generational gap has yet to become a visible threat to the industry. Yang Yao has certainly seen young people refuse the trade in favour of livestreaming or something else, but walk into a furniture factory and you still find plenty of strongly built young men working bare-chested — a fact closely tied to the shape of China’s population by level of education.
strings.p84: “In the Chinese labour market there are a great many people who left school at primary or junior-high level. Their options are limited, so going into a factory to learn a trade becomes the main route, and furniture absorbs a lot of that basic labour,” Yang Yao says.
strings.p85: More to the point, the pay is a genuine draw. When he first entered the Chinese market sixteen years ago, Yang Yao recalls, a general labourer or unskilled hand in a furniture factory earned around RMB 800 to 900 a month; today, without RMB 4,000 to 5,000 you will struggle to hire anyone. A skilled craftsman once earned a few thousand yuan a month and can now make RMB 10,000 to 20,000.
strings.p86: Official figures published by China’s National Bureau of Statistics for 2025 put national per-capita disposable income at roughly RMB 43,000 a year, or about RMB 3,600 a month. Against that, a skilled furniture craftsman clearing over RMB 10,000 is an obvious incentive.
strings.p87: Rising wages signal that demand for labour in Chinese furniture manufacturing remains strong — and they have also shifted the assumption that factory work means low pay. For some young people, learning a trade on the floor and working up to craftsman offers a route to steady income without the educational threshold other careers demand. It is why the industry can still find front-line workers, and why its labour structure looks nothing like Taiwan’s.
strings.p88: When young people keep entering the factories and working their way up over years from labourer to craftsman, the shop floor accumulates a reasonably complete chain of transmitted skill — one that does not snap when a generation turns over, and that shows in both the efficiency and the quality of what gets made. For China’s furniture industry, the size of the population is not only a market advantage; it is what sustains the workforce and the passing-on of technique.
strings.p89: Rising wages have, admittedly, pushed a number of Chinese factories to relocate to Southeast Asia. As Yang Yao sees it, though, furniture manufacturing there is still at a relatively early, batch-production stage. Judged on the craftsmanship and the flexibility that bespoke work requires, the technique Chinese craftsmen have built up over years remains hard to replace any time soon.
strings.p90: Taiwan, by contrast, has a population structure, an education profile, a set of salary expectations and an industrial scale that together give talent in related fields pause before going into furniture making and design.
strings.p91: The unevenness of what circulates on Xiaohongshu has been felt keenly by Ho Ming-hsun, an interior designer of twenty-eight years who still takes commissions. The platform gives people far more exposure to design — and just as easily leaves them believing the expertise involved has somehow become optional, so that they arrive with renovation requests wildly beyond their budget, or simply beyond reality.
strings.p92: Interior design, Ho explains, moves through four stages: structural work, construction, decoration and finishing. Each breaks down into several trades — masonry alone covers blockwork, waterproofing, flooring and tiling; window and door work covers metalwork, aluminium frames and steel doors. He sets out what a site actually involves: “A job with more than twenty trades and hundreds of people in it is not expertise that a short video can replace.”
strings.p93: Brother De, design director at an interior design firm, posted his first renovation walkthrough on YouTube eight years ago; the channel now has more than 70,000 subscribers and some 3,000 videos. He has spent years studying how design circulates online, and has made several videos about what appears on Xiaohongshu. Much of it, he says, stops at an idealised concept, and running into Taiwanese regulations and building structures is where it fails. “Take the wall-building videos on Xiaohongshu — most of that isn’t legal here. Any change touching the structure has to be professionally assessed. Even an architect isn’t necessarily fluent in structural calculation; you need a structural engineer to work out the concrete strength and the load the rebar will take.”
strings.p94: Design trends may follow the international mood, but landing them is a thoroughly local expertise. Users who cannot judge how professional a piece of content is sometimes fall back on counting examples instead, which breeds a distrust — and a disregard — for the profession itself. One Threads user, having seen a run of Xiaohongshu renovations, wrote: “Honestly, if the mainlanders came for Taiwanese jobs, about 80 per cent of us would be out.”
strings.p95: In the replies, other users pointed out that the interiors he had posted came originally from a European design firm — lifted, with no credit. Which says something about the scale of image theft on the platform.
strings.p96: Some accounts function mainly as couriers, carrying material that cannot be found on the Chinese internet onto Xiaohongshu. The motive may be nothing worse than sharing a style they like; it may be deliberate theft. At the mild end, the source is noted obliquely, tucked into a corner where nobody looks. At the other end, someone else’s work is simply claimed as their own.
strings.p97: Interior designer Chang Ning once worked with a landscape team in Shanghai. She was impressed by how fast and how efficiently they executed, but she also notes that the two sides use a great deal of different professional vocabulary, which can become a hidden cost in day-to-day collaboration. In one client conversation she was asked for a tile called “soft-light tile” — which turns out to be nothing more than a Xiaohongshu coinage for a certain kind of tile, with no formal equivalent in Taiwan.
strings.p98: Arguing with a client about terminology is not what a designer is for, Chang says. So once she understood what the client actually wanted, she specified a Taiwanese tile with a comparable texture and finish, and arrived at much the same effect.
strings.p99: And while style is how most lay people first meet interior design through social media, it is not how trained designers understand their work. Huang Hsiao-jung studied interior design, worked at three firms and now designs at an architecture practice. “When someone talks to a designer about style, honestly, it’s foreign to us.” Courses, she explains, do not sort design into styles for students to learn one by one. They go back to what a space and the people in it fundamentally need.
strings.p100: “If I’m designing a house for three generations under one roof, I’m thinking about how they can be together and interact in the same space while still keeping somewhere of their own. You start from that and develop the whole design out of it.” Interior design, as Huang sees it, is closer to building an experience of space than to the materials, colours and visual effects on the surface. How people feel inside it is the core the whole thing rests on; every material, every fall of light, every path through the rooms exists to produce that experience.
strings.p101: Much of the vocabulary on Xiaohongshu sounds at first like an extension of professional design. More often it is a label a creator has invented to satisfy the algorithm.
strings.p102: Elvy, a soft-furnishings consultant, says a client arriving with Xiaohongshu screenshots genuinely helps the early, divergent hunt for ideas — but after the conversation it falls to the designer to narrow things down and deliver on quality, lead times and materials. For her own inspiration she prefers European websites and magazines, a way of keeping her eye trained and of not letting long exposure to cheap imitations erode her taste.
strings.p103: If “planting grass” is the seeding of desire, “weeding” is what follows: the shopper, having absorbed the content, either lets the urge go or places the order and satisfies it. Kiki has done her share of weeding, and a Xiaohongshu aesthetic called “ready-to-run” became the thing that made her rethink what she needed at home.
strings.p104: Kiki’s attachment to the platform began at university, and it had to do with being an only child. Against the backdrop of China’s one-child policy, Xiaohongshu carries a great deal of discussion among only children, and her own unplaceable anxieties found somewhere to settle in it. As her life moved on, so did what she followed: less about feelings and growing up, more about how to arrange and plan the space she lived in.
strings.p105: There are people on Xiaohongshu, Kiki says, who advocate a “ready-to-run” style, built on the idea that a home should be portable — no excess decoration, nothing bulky taking up room. Some skip tables and chairs altogether, using a low cabinet as a table and sitting on the floor: minimalism carried to its limit. Minimalism was already the direction Kiki wanted, though she never set out to travel all the way along that spectrum. Trying to reproduce a home with the right <button class="term" type="button" data-term="網感">online-ready look</button>, she started out reading enormous numbers of posts — and all that information did not bring the ideal closer. It mostly added pressure. “You have to spend a lot of money buying a lot of things, which completely contradicts why I liked minimalism in the first place.”
strings.p106: She also began to notice that the most polished bloggers were all running the same play: similar furniture, similar arrangements, and a path leading the reader to the seller’s shop. The technique — sharing in appearance, selling in fact — gradually cost them her trust. The people posting “ready-to-run” content, by contrast, were mostly students and amateurs, and it was their lived practice and plain honesty that Kiki came to find worth following.
strings.p107: “Ready-to-run,” she says, is a reminder that you do not have to chase a beautifully styled room, or let a consumer-driven idea of taste dictate to you. “Your home shouldn’t be something that can be sold through.”
strings.p108: Fumio Sasaki, the Japanese author of Goodbye, Things, argues that in the internet age our heads are stuffed with information we do not need and we care far too much about how we look to others, pouring our energy into wanting things and then managing them — a long expenditure of effort for brief pleasure, which makes what actually matters hard to see. The exhaustion that follows is where minimalism begins. “This trend,” he writes, “is not a passing whim or a longing for a different lifestyle. The reasons behind it are more practical than that.”
strings.p109: An overwhelming abundance of information is a product of commercialism, and minimalism is a response to it; minimalist interiors are that philosophy put into practice. Yet minimalism is so often hitched to the “happiness” of decluttering that it has become a marketing device in its own right. Sellers take the idea, raise the banner of wanting less, and run a consumption trap off the back of it. Type “minimalist furniture” into Taobao’s search bar and the results are endless — which is its own kind of joke.
strings.p110: Even so, Taobao has been company to Shaobai through a low period.
strings.p111: He used to be a man who wanted sports cars and luxury goods, and the chase ate away at his mental health. Then the way he shopped on Taobao overturned what he thought pleasure required. “It turns out this little money can bring this much satisfaction.” On the other end of the video call, Shaobai turns a pair of sharply styled sunglasses over in his hands. They cost under NT$20, and the pleasure they give him is not one bit smaller than a million-dollar car.

glossary.Z 世代: Broadly, those born between the late 1990s and the early 2010s, who grew up as the internet, smartphones and social media took hold — hence the alternative label “digital natives.” Research bodies differ slightly on the exact birth years.
glossary.平替: Chinese internet slang for a cheaper substitute: a product that costs less but can stand in for the original in function, effect or style. Roughly, a “dupe.”
glossary.3D渲染圖: A computer-generated image that uses 3D modelling to simulate how a finished interior will look, based on dimensions, materials, furniture layout and lighting. It is used to present and discuss a design — it is not a photograph of completed work.
glossary.頭部家具買家: Buyers who know the production regions, the factories and the supply chain intimately, and who build a following by posting factory tours, source-hunting tips and warnings about what to avoid — influence they then bring to bear on other people’s purchasing decisions.
glossary.狼性: A term common in Chinese business and internet usage, borrowed from the competitive, co-operative behaviour of wolf packs. It describes a workplace culture built on competition, ambition, speed of execution and sheer intensity — and is often used of long hours, instant responsiveness and a relentless focus on results.
glossary.卷: Chinese internet slang, from the academic term “involution.” It describes a market — whether the competition is over price, performance or sheer hours worked — in which everyone keeps pouring in more time, energy and money without any matching return.
glossary.限高: In China, a person placed on the courts’ register of defaulters over unpaid debts, who has not met the obligations set out in a binding judgment, can be subjected to consumption restrictions: barred from flights and high-speed rail, and from high-value spending beyond what daily life and work require.
glossary.貨款: The sum a buyer owes a seller for goods, on the terms the two sides have agreed.
glossary.圖紙: Drawings that set out a piece of furniture’s form, structure and method of construction in diagrams and dimensions, used as the basis for design and manufacture.
glossary.私人集運: A third-party forwarder that receives, inspects and consolidates a shopper’s purchases from Chinese e-commerce platforms before shipping them on to Taiwan. Compared with a platform’s own delivery, forwarders usually offer more flexible freight rates, parcel consolidation and handling of awkward items — but the risk of damage, loss and after-sales disputes falls on the buyer.
glossary.包郵: A listing whose price already covers delivery within a specified area, so the buyer pays no separate shipping fee. Free shipping is a staple promotion on Chinese e-commerce platforms.
glossary.文公尺: Also known as the Luban ruler, the measuring rule used in traditional carpentry and furniture making. As well as giving dimensions, it divides the scale into auspicious and inauspicious bands. Furniture, doors and windows built to lucky measurements are held to bring good fortune, so craftsmen use it to steer clear of the unlucky ones.
glossary.封號: When a social or e-commerce platform restricts or permanently disables an account for breaking its rules, posting prohibited content or triggering other risk flags. A banned account may be unable to log in, post or reach its followers, and the traffic and commercial value built up on it can be lost with it.
glossary.起號: Chinese social and e-commerce jargon for building an account from nothing — posting consistently, accumulating followers and traffic, and growing the account’s reach and commercial value step by step. Common on Douyin, Xiaohongshu and similar platforms.
glossary.網感: Chinese internet slang for a feel for what travels online: an instinct for current trends, platform culture and the tastes of younger users. Something with it tends to have a strong visual identity, to be easy to share and to be worth photographing — the qualities that get noticed on Xiaohongshu or Douyin.
